paragraphs.heading: What a hotspot is
paragraphs.text: A hotspot is a volcanic area thought to be fed by mantle beneath it that is unusually hot compared with the mantle around it. Hawaii, Iceland and Yellowstone are examples. Where a hotspot sits on the Earth's surface does not depend on the boundaries of tectonic plates. The concept has been used to explain the origin of volcanism wherever it has no link to a constructive or destructive plate margin.

paragraphs.heading: How the idea began
paragraphs.text: The concept goes back to the work of J. Tuzo Wilson. In 1963 he proposed that the Hawaiian Islands formed as a tectonic plate moved slowly across a hot region beneath the surface. Later came the proposal that streams of hot mantle feed hotspots, rising from the boundary between the Earth's core and mantle in a structure called a mantle plume. Whether such plumes exist has been a major controversy in Earth science, though seismic images consistent with the evolving theory now exist.

paragraphs.heading: Two competing explanations
paragraphs.text: Two hypotheses try to explain where hotspots come from. In the first, hotspots are caused by mantle plumes that rise from the core–mantle boundary. The second, called the plate theory, holds that the mantle beneath a hotspot is not unusually hot. In that view the crust above is unusually weak or thin, and melt rises passively from shallow depths.

paragraphs.heading: Chains of volcanoes
paragraphs.text: A hotspot may build a chain of volcanoes as the plates move above it. The combined plume and hotspot hypothesis originally pictured the feeding structures as fixed relative to one another, while continents and seafloor drifted overhead. It therefore predicts chains of volcanoes whose ages progress along the chain. In the Hawaiian archipelago the islands get progressively older and more deeply eroded toward the northwest. Yellowstone is the last in a chain of extinct calderas that get progressively older toward the west.

paragraphs.heading: A tracking tool with problems
paragraphs.text: Geologists have tried to use these chains to track how the Earth's tectonic plates move. The effort has run into trouble. Very long chains are lacking, many chains, the Galápagos for example, are not time-progressive, and hotspots do not seem to stay fixed relative to each other. The plumes imaged so far also differ from what many expected: they differ widely in width and other characteristics, and they are tilted, not simple, fairly narrow and purely thermal. Only Yellowstone has so far been consistently modelled and imaged all the way from the deep mantle to the surface.

paragraphs.heading: A different origin from island arcs
paragraphs.text: Hotspot volcanoes are thought to originate in a fundamentally different way from island arc volcanoes. Island arc volcanoes form over subduction zones, at boundaries where plates converge. When one oceanic plate meets another, the denser one is forced down into a deep ocean trench. As it goes down it releases water into the base of the plate above. The water mixes with the rock and changes its composition, causing some rock to melt and rise. This is what fuels volcanic chains like the Aleutian Islands, near Alaska.

paragraphs.heading: Less explosive, with exceptions
paragraphs.text: Most hotspot volcanoes are basaltic, as in Hawaii and Tahiti. That makes them less explosive than the volcanoes of subduction zones, where water is trapped under the overriding plate. Hotspots in continental regions are another matter. There, basaltic magma comes up through continental crust, and the crust melts to form rhyolites, which can produce violent eruptions. The Yellowstone Caldera, for example, was created by volcanic explosions that rank among the most powerful in geologic history.
